stem: An online shop sends its parcels with three couriers. Courier X takes 50% of the parcels, courier Y takes 30% and courier Z takes the rest. The probability that a parcel arrives late is 0.04 with X, 0.1 with Y and 0.05 with Z.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that a parcel chosen at random arrives late.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A parcel arrives late. Find the probability that it was sent with courier Y.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A parcel arrives on time. Find the probability that it was sent with courier X.

idea: Bayes’ theorem turns the probabilities around: \(P(Y \mid \text{late}) = \dfrac{P(Y \cap \text{late})}{P(\text{late})}\). The bottom line is the total probability of being late, added over all three couriers.

stem: A disease affects 1% of the trees in a forest. A test for the disease gives a positive result for 90% of diseased trees and for 5% of healthy trees.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that a tree chosen at random gives a positive result.

parts.label: b
parts.text: A tree gives a positive result. Find the probability that it has the disease. Give your answer as a fraction.
Each tree that gives a positive result is tested a second time. Given whether or not a tree has the disease, the results of its two tests are independent.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A tree gives a positive result in both tests. Find the probability that it has the disease.

idea: Most positive results come from the many healthy trees, so one positive result is weak evidence. For two tests, multiply the conditional probabilities along each branch: a diseased tree tests positive twice with probability \(0.9^2\), a healthy tree with probability \(0.05^2\).

stem: At a school, 40% of the students walk to school, 35% cycle and the rest come by bus. The probability that a student is late is 0.05 for those who walk, 0.02 for those who cycle and \(p\) for those who come by bus.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find, in terms of \(p\), the probability that a student chosen at random is late.
Given that a student is late, the probability that the student came by bus is 0.5.

parts.label: c
parts.text: A student is late. Find the probability that the student walked to school.

idea: Write the conditional probability as a fraction with the total probability of being late underneath, and solve the resulting equation for \(p\).

stem: A box contains three coins. One coin is fair, one has a head on both sides, and one is biased so that it shows a head with probability \(\dfrac{1}{4}\). A coin is taken from the box at random and tossed twice. It shows a head both times.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that a coin taken at random shows two heads in two tosses.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the coin is the one with a head on both sides.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The same coin is tossed a third time. Find the probability that it shows a head.

idea: After seeing two heads, update the probability of each coin with Bayes’ theorem. The chance of a third head is then an average of the three coins’ head probabilities, weighted by these updated probabilities.

solution.label: c
steps: In the same way, \(P(\text{fair} \mid HH) = \dfrac{\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{4}}{\frac{7}{16}} = \dfrac{4}{21}\) and \(P(\text{biased} \mid HH) = \dfrac{\frac{1}{3} \times \frac{1}{16}}{\frac{7}{16}} = \dfrac{1}{21}\).

stem: A factory makes components in batches. 90% of batches are good, and in a good batch each component is faulty with probability 0.02. The other 10% of batches are poor, and in a poor batch each component is faulty with probability 0.1. An inspector tests a random sample of 20 components from a batch. Components are faulty independently of each other.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the sample contains at least 2 faulty components when the batch is good, and when the batch is poor.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the sample from a batch chosen at random contains at least 2 faulty components.

parts.label: c
parts.text: The sample contains at least 2 faulty components. Find the probability that the batch is poor.
The inspector rejects a batch when the sample contains at least 2 faulty components, and accepts it otherwise.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the probability that a batch chosen at random is wrongly judged, that is, a good batch is rejected or a poor batch is accepted.

idea: Given the type of batch, the number of faulty components in the sample is binomial. Bayes’ theorem then reverses the condition. A wrong judgement is one of two separate events, so add their probabilities.

solution.label: d
steps: Good and rejected: \(0.9 \times 0.05989\ldots = 0.05390\ldots\) Poor and accepted: \(0.1 \times (1 - 0.60825\ldots) = 0.03917\ldots\)

stem: Die A is an ordinary fair six-sided die with faces 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. Die B is a fair six-sided die with faces 2, 3, 3, 4, 4 and 5. Let \(X\) be the score on die A and \(Y\) the score on die B.
idea: Use \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \left[E(X)\right]^2\). Two dice can have the same mean but different spreads.

stem: The discrete random variable \(X\) has \(P(X = x) = \dfrac{c}{x}\), for \(x = 1, 2, 3, 6\), where \(c\) is a constant.
idea: The probabilities add to 1. In \(E(X) = \sum x \, P(X = x)\) and \(E(X^2) = \sum x^2 \, P(X = x)\), the factor \(\dfrac{1}{x}\) cancels, which makes the sums short.

solution.label: b
steps: \(E(X) = \sum x \times \dfrac{c}{x} = 4c\), since there are four values.

stem: A fair coin is tossed until it shows a head, but it is tossed no more than three times. Let \(X\) be the number of tosses.
idea: \(X = 1\) or \(2\) needs the first head on that toss. \(X = 3\) happens whenever the first two tosses are tails, whatever the third toss shows.

stem: The random variable \(X\) takes the values 1, 2 and \(k\), where \(k > 2\), with probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 respectively.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Given that \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = 2.29\), find the value of \(k\).

idea: Work out \(E(X^2)\) in terms of \(k\) and subtract the square of the mean. The variance condition then gives a quadratic in \(k\); the condition \(k > 2\) picks the root.

stem: Two games at a fair each cost $2 to play.
In game A, the player wins $5 with probability 0.4 and otherwise wins nothing.
In game B, the player wins $\(x\) with probability 0.1, wins $1 with probability 0.5, and otherwise wins nothing.
The profit is the amount won minus the $2 paid.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the mean and the standard deviation of the profit in game A.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Game B is fair, which means that the expected profit is zero. Find the value of \(x\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the standard deviation of the profit in game B.

idea: List each profit with its probability. Both games have mean profit zero, so the standard deviation is what tells them apart: it measures how far a player’s results swing.

solution.label: a
steps: Mean: \(1.2 - 1.2 = 0\). \(E(G^2) = 0.4 \times 9 + 0.6 \times 4 = 6\), so the variance is 6 and the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{6} = 2.449\ldots\)

solution.label: b
steps: Expected winnings must equal the $2 cost: \(0.1x + 0.5 \times 1 = 2\).

solution.label: c
steps: Profit 13 with probability 0.1, \(-1\) with probability 0.5, \(-2\) with probability 0.4.
\(E(G^2) = 0.1 \times 169 + 0.5 \times 1 + 0.4 \times 4 = 19\), and the mean is 0, so the standard deviation is \(\sqrt{19} = 4.358\ldots\)

stem: The random variable \(X\) has \(E(X) = 5\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4\).
idea: \(E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b\) and \(\mathrm{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)\). Adding a constant moves the values but does not spread them, and a negative \(a\) still gives a positive variance.

stem: In a city in July, the daily maximum temperature, \(C\) °C, has mean 20 and standard deviation 5. The temperature in degrees Fahrenheit is \(F = 1.8C + 32\).
idea: \(F\) is a linear function of \(C\). The added 32 shifts the mean only; the factor 1.8 multiplies the standard deviation.

stem: The reading, \(X\), from a sensor has mean 12 and standard deviation 3. The sensor is recalibrated, so that the new reading for the same measurement is \(Y = aX + b\), where \(a > 0\). The new readings have mean 20 and standard deviation 4.5.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of \(a\) and the value of \(b\).

idea: The standard deviation scales by \(a\), which gives \(a\); the mean then gives \(b\). A linear function of a normal variable is normal. For part (c), write \(2Y - X\) in terms of \(X\) alone: it is one random variable, not two independent ones.

stem: The random variable \(X\) has mean \(\mu\). It is given that \(E\left((X - 1)^2\right) = 10\) and \(E\left((X + 1)^2\right) = 18\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the value of \(\mu\) and the value of \(E(X^2)\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that \(E\left((X - c)^2\right) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + (\mu - c)^2\) for any constant \(c\), and hence find the least possible value of \(E\left((X - c)^2\right)\).

idea: Expectation is linear: \(E\left((X - 1)^2\right) = E(X^2) - 2E(X) + 1\). Two such equations give \(E(X)\) and \(E(X^2)\). Part (c) shows that the mean is the point about which the average squared distance is smallest.

solution.label: c
steps: \((\mu - c)^2 \geq 0\), with equality when \(c = \mu = 2\). So the least value is \(\mathrm{Var}(X)\).

stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = kx^3\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 2\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.
idea: The total area under a probability density function is 1. A probability is the area under the curve over the interval.

stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = \dfrac{k}{x^2}\) for \(1 \leq x \leq 4\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.
idea: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{1}{x^2}\,dx = -\frac{1}{x}\). For the conditional probability, the event \(X > 3\) lies inside \(X > 2\), so \(P(X > 3 \mid X > 2) = \dfrac{P(X > 3)}{P(X > 2)}\).

stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = k\mathrm{e}^{-x/2}\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 2\ln 3\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.
idea: \(\displaystyle\int \mathrm{e}^{-x/2}\,dx = -2\mathrm{e}^{-x/2}\), and \(\mathrm{e}^{-\ln 3} = \dfrac{1}{3}\).

stem: The continuous random variable \(T\) has probability density function \(f(t) = \dfrac{k}{1 + t^2}\) for \(0 \leq t \leq \sqrt{3}\), and \(f(t) = 0\) otherwise.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the value of \(a\) for which \(P(T < a) = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

idea: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{1}{1 + t^2}\,dt = \arctan t\). Learn the exact values \(\arctan 1 = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\arctan\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\).

stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = \dfrac{k}{x + 1}\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 3\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that the median of \(X\) is 1.

idea: \(\displaystyle\int \frac{1}{x + 1}\,dx = \ln(x + 1)\), and \(\ln 4 = 2\ln 2\). The median \(m\) satisfies \(P(X < m) = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

subtopic: Averages and spread of continuous random variables
stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = \dfrac{x}{8}\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 4\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.
idea: The mode is where the density is greatest. The median \(m\) cuts the area in half. The mean is \(\displaystyle\int x f(x)\,dx\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(f\) is increasing, so it is greatest at the right end.

subtopic: Averages and spread of continuous random variables
stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = kx^2(3 - x)\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 3\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.
idea: The mode is the value of \(x\) where \(f\) has its maximum, so differentiate and set \(f'(x) = 0\). Expand the brackets before integrating.

solution.label: b
steps: \(f'(x) = k(6x - 3x^2) = 3kx(2 - x)\), which is zero at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\). \(f(0) = 0\), and \(f\) rises then falls on \([0, 3]\), so the maximum is at \(x = 2\).

subtopic: Averages and spread of continuous random variables
stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = \dfrac{3(x^2 + 2)}{20}\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 2\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.
idea: \(\mathrm{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - \left[E(X)\right]^2\), with \(E(X^2) = \displaystyle\int x^2 f(x)\,dx\). The median leads to a cubic equation, which a calculator solves.

solution.label: c
steps: The only real solution is \(m = 1.3002\ldots\), which lies in \([0, 2]\).

idea: Areas of the rectangle and the triangle give \(k\) without integrating. Check which piece the median lies in before solving for it. The mean needs one integral for each piece.

solution.label: b
steps: The rectangle has area \(\dfrac{4}{7} > \dfrac{1}{2}\), so the median \(m\) is in \([0, 2)\): \(\dfrac{2m}{7} = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

solution.label: d
steps: \(\dfrac{13}{7} < 2\), so \(P\left(X > \dfrac{13}{7}\right) = \dfrac{2}{7}\left(2 - \dfrac{13}{7}\right) + \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{2}{49} + \dfrac{21}{49}\), where \(\dfrac{3}{7}\) is the area of the triangle.

stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = kx^n\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 1\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise, where \(n > 0\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: The median of \(X\) is 0.9. Find the value of \(n\), and hence find \(E(X)\).

idea: The integrals are powers of \(x\), evaluated at 1. For the median, \(P(X < 0.9) = 0.9^{n+1} = 0.5\); take logarithms to find \(n\).

subtopic: Averages and spread of continuous random variables
stem: The continuous random variable \(X\) has probability density function \(f(x) = \dfrac{3(4 - x)^2}{64}\) for \(0 \leq x \leq 4\), and \(f(x) = 0\) otherwise.
idea: The substitution \(u = 4 - x\) makes every integral a sum of powers of \(u\). For the median, the area to the right of \(m\) is \(\dfrac{(4 - m)^3}{64}\).

solution.label: a
steps: \(f\) decreases on \([0, 4]\), so it is greatest at \(x = 0\).

stem: The six letters of the word ORANGE are arranged in a row in a random order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the arrangement begins with a vowel.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the three vowels are next to each other.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that the vowels appear in the order A, E, O, reading from left to right (not necessarily next to each other).

idea: There are \(6! = 720\) equally likely arrangements. Treat letters that must stay together as one block. For part (c), each of the \(3!\) orders of the vowels is equally likely.

solution.label: a
steps: 3 of the 6 letters (O, A, E) are vowels, and each letter is equally likely to come first.

solution.label: b
steps: Arrange the block and R, N, G: \(4!\) ways. Arrange the vowels in the block: \(3!\) ways.

solution.label: c
steps: The three vowels appear in one of \(3! = 6\) orders, all equally likely, and only one is A, E, O.

stem: A drawer contains 5 pairs of socks, and no two pairs are alike. Four socks are taken from the drawer at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of ways of choosing four socks from the drawer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that no two of the four socks make a pair.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that the four socks contain exactly one pair.

idea: Count choices of pairs first, then choose a sock from each pair. For “no pair”, choose 4 of the 5 pairs and one sock from each.

solution.label: b
steps: Choose 4 of the 5 pairs, then 1 sock from each: \(\dbinom{5}{4} \times 2^4 = 80\).

solution.label: c
steps: Choose the complete pair: 5 ways. Choose 2 of the other 4 pairs: \(\dbinom{4}{2} = 6\) ways, and one sock from each: \(2^2 = 4\).

stem: In a lottery, a player chooses 5 different numbers from 1 to 25. Then 5 different winning numbers are drawn at random from 1 to 25.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the number of different sets of 5 winning numbers.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that the player’s numbers match all 5 winning numbers.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the probability that exactly 3 of the player’s numbers are winning numbers.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Find the probability that at least 3 of the player’s numbers are winning numbers.

idea: Every set of 5 winning numbers is equally likely. To match exactly 3, the draw must contain 3 of the player’s 5 numbers and 2 of the other 20 numbers.

solution.label: b
steps: Only one of the sets matches.

stem: Eight people, including three friends Amir, Bo and Cleo, sit in a row of eight seats in a random order.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Find the probability that the three friends sit next to each other.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the probability that no two of the three friends sit next to each other.

idea: For (a), glue the three friends into one block. For (b), seat the other five people first; this makes 6 gaps (including both ends), and the friends must go in 3 different gaps.

solution.label: a
steps: The block and the other 5 people: \(6!\) orders. The friends within the block: \(3!\) orders.

solution.label: b
steps: Arrange the other five: \(5! = 120\) ways. Choose 3 of the 6 gaps: \(\dbinom{6}{3} = 20\). Put the friends in them in order: \(3! = 6\).

stem: Assume that a person is equally likely to be born in any of the 12 months, independently of other people.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Three people are chosen. Find the probability that they were born in three different months.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Four people are chosen. Find the probability that at least two of them were born in the same month.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the least number of people for which the probability that at least two of them were born in the same month is more than 0.9.

idea: Count the ways for everyone to be in different months: \(12 \times 11 \times 10 \times \ldots\). “At least two the same” is the complement of “all different”.

solution.label: c
steps: For \(n\) people the probability is \(1 - \dfrac{12 \times 11 \times \cdots \times (13 - n)}{12^n}\).
